headings.title: Introduction to the Vascular System
headings.content: The vascular system functions as a closed transport network delivering oxygen, hormones, and nutrients to tissues while removing metabolic waste products. This circulatory highway spans two primary loops. The pulmonary circuit transports deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange, returning oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium. Meanwhile, the systemic circuit pumps oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to every organ system, collecting carbon dioxide before returning it via the venae cavae to the right atrium. Without this continuous perfusion, cellular hypoxia and necrosis follow rapidly, making vascular integrity vital to homeostatic balance.

headings.title: Arteries and Arterioles
headings.content: Arteries withstand high-pressure pulsatile flow propelled directly by ventricular contraction. Elastic arteries like the aorta feature thick walls rich in elastin fibers, allowing them to stretch during systole and recoil during diastole to maintain steady downstream flow. Muscular arteries distribute blood to specific organ beds, possessing prominent smooth muscle layers capable of powerful vasomotion. Arterioles represent the final microscopic branches of the arterial tree. Acting as the primary resistance vessels of the vascular network, arterioles regulate systemic blood pressure and determine capillary bed perfusion through local constriction and dilation.

headings.title: Capillaries
headings.content:
Capillaries form extensive microscopic networks where nutrient, gas, and fluid exchange occurs between the blood and interstitial fluid. Structurally, their walls consist of a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basal lamina, minimizing the diffusion distance to the barest minimum.

- **Continuous capillaries**: Feature an uninterrupted endothelial lining joined by tight junctions, found predominantly in skin, muscle, and the blood-brain barrier.
- **Fenestrated capillaries**: Contain small pores or fenestrations allowing high-volume fluid exchange, typical in endocrine glands, intestines, and renal glomeruli.
- **Sinusoid capillaries**: Display large intercellular gaps and incomplete basement membranes, permitting the passage of whole cells in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

headings.title: Venules and Veins
headings.content: After passing through capillary beds, blood enters postcapillary venules and converges into progressively larger veins on its return journey to the heart. Operating under low pressure, veins hold approximately sixty percent of the total blood volume at rest, serving as an adaptable blood reservoir. To overcome gravity and prevent backflow, medium and large veins in the limbs contain delicate endothelial folds forming one-way valves. Venous return is further assisted by the skeletal muscle pump—where contracting limb muscles squeeze deep veins—and the respiratory pump, which creates negative thoracic pressure during inspiration to draw blood toward the right atrium.

headings.title: Histology and Structure of Blood Vessel Walls
headings.content:
Most blood vessels share a trilaminar wall architecture, though the relative thickness of each layer varies depending on vessel type and function.

| Vessel Layer | Primary Histological Components | Main Functional Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tunica Intima** | Simple squamous endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue | Provides a friction-reducing lining and secretes paracrine factors |
| **Tunica Media** | Circular smooth muscle and variable amounts of elastin/collagen | Regulates lumen diameter and withstands blood pressure |
| **Tunica Externa** | Dense irregular connective tissue with vasa vasorum | Anchors vessels to surrounding tissue and supplies vessel wall cells |

In clinical practice, damage to the delicate tunica intima triggers platelet aggregation and the clotting cascade, which initiates atherosclerosis or localized thrombosis.

headings.title: Hemodynamics and Blood Flow Regulation
headings.content: Blood flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient between two points and inversely proportional to vascular resistance. According to Poiseuille's law, vessel radius exerts a massive influence on resistance—even minor vasoconstriction drastically reduces flow, while vasodilation multiplies it. Mean arterial pressure is determined by cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance. Neural control via the vasomotor center in the medulla oblongata adjusts vessel tone, while hormonal regulators like aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system manage long-term blood volume and pressure.

headings.title: Common Vascular Disorders in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Vascular pathology frequently stems from structural degeneration, chronic inflammation, or abnormal clotting. Atherosclerosis involves lipid plaques accumulating within the tunica intima of medium and large arteries, narrowing the lumen and predisposing patients to ischemia, myocardial infarction, or stroke. Chronic venous insufficiency occurs when valve incompetence in lower limb veins causes blood pooling, resulting in edema, skin hyperpigmentation, and painful ulcerations. Aneurysms represent localized wall ballooning caused by structural weakness, carrying a severe risk of rupture and fatal hemorrhage. Nurses caring for these patients must regularly assess peripheral pulses, capillary refill, and tissue perfusion.
